questions.q: What determines which shard a Kinesis Data Streams record is written to?
options: The consumer that will eventually read it
A round-robin assignment across all shards
The record's partition key, hashed by Kinesis
The order the record was produced in
questions.explain: Kinesis hashes the partition key you supply on each record to pick a shard — same key, same shard, every time.

questions.q: Within a Kinesis data stream, ordering is guaranteed:
options: Across the entire stream regardless of shard
Only when using the Kinesis Client Library
Only if you disable partition keys
Within a single shard, not across the whole stream
questions.explain: Records are strictly ordered within the shard they land on. Ordering across the whole stream isn't guaranteed unless every relevant record shares a partition key and therefore a shard.

questions.q: What is a shard's approximate write throughput limit?
options: 1 GB/second, unlimited records
Shards have no throughput limit
100 KB/second, 10 records/second
1 MB/second or 1,000 records/second
questions.explain: Each shard caps out at 1 MB/second or 1,000 records/second in, whichever limit is hit first.

questions.q: What does the Kinesis Client Library (KCL) handle for a consumer application?
options: Shard discovery, load balancing across workers, and checkpointing
Automatically provisioning new AWS accounts
Converting the stream into an S3 bucket
Compressing records before they're written to the stream
questions.explain: The KCL is a client-side library that manages the operational details of consuming a stream — discovering shards, balancing them across worker instances, and tracking each worker's read position.

questions.q: Why does a stream's retention period matter for downstream consumers?
options: It controls which AWS region the stream runs in
It determines how many shards the stream can have
It lets a consumer replay or reprocess records within that window instead of losing them after one read
It sets the maximum size of a single record
questions.explain: Unlike a plain queue, Kinesis keeps records readable for the retention period (24 hours by default, extendable to 365 days), so multiple consumers can read independently and a lagging or failed consumer can rewind.
